subChunks.title: Social Influence: Conformity & Obedience
subChunks.hookHtml: On 18 November 1978, in a remote jungle settlement in Guyana, 918 members of the Peoples Temple — nearly a third of them children — died by ingesting cyanide-laced fruit punch at the instruction of their leader, Jim Jones. Many drank willingly. Others watched friends and family members die first, then drank. Social psychologists have spent decades asking: how? How do ordinary people, in groups, do things they would never do alone? The answer is uncomfortable — because the factors that led to Jonestown are not exceptional. They operate every day, in workplaces, schools, and families. Social psychology is the science of how other people — their presence, their expectations, their authority — shape what we think, feel, and do. Understanding social influence is among the most practically important knowledge psychology offers.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Conformity: Asch's Line Studies

Solomon Asch (1951) conducted a deceptively simple experiment. Participants were asked to judge which of three comparison lines matched a standard line in length — an easy perceptual task with an obvious correct answer. However, the participant was seated with a group of confederates who, on certain trials, unanimously gave a clearly wrong answer.

Results: 75% of participants conformed to the incorrect majority on at least one trial; overall conformity rate was approximately 32%. In the control condition (no social pressure), errors occurred less than 1% of the time. Asch identified two mechanisms:

  • Informational social influence: Conforming because you genuinely believe the group knows better — particularly likely in ambiguous situations or when the task is difficult.
  • Normative social influence: Conforming to avoid rejection or social disapproval, even when you privately disagree. Post-study interviews revealed many participants conformed while knowing the group was wrong.

Variables affecting conformity: Group size (maximum conformity with 3–4 people; additional members add little), unanimity (a single ally drastically reduces conformity), difficulty of task (ambiguity increases informational influence), and individual factors (self-esteem, need for approval).

Evaluation: The studies used an artificial task with strangers — conformity to close peers on real-world decisions may operate differently. Perrin and Spencer (1980) replicated with British engineering students and found dramatically lower conformity, suggesting cultural variation. The studies also did not measure long-term attitude change, only public compliance.

Obedience: Milgram's Shock Studies

Stanley Milgram's (1963–1974) series of studies remains the most famous — and most ethically controversial — in psychology's history. Participants believed they were 'teachers' administering escalating electric shocks to a 'learner' (confederate) whenever a wrong answer was given. Despite scripted protests and ultimately silence from the learner, 65% of participants in the baseline condition administered the maximum 450 volts.

Factors increasing obedience:

  • Physical and psychological proximity to authority (experimenter present, not just on phone)
  • Remoteness of the victim (less obedience when learner was visible)
  • Prestige of the institution (Yale University conferred legitimacy)
  • Agentic state: participants felt they were acting as an instrument of authority, not as moral agents
  • Gradual commitment: 'foot in the door' — starting with small shocks made escalation feel incremental

Evaluation: Milgram's findings have replicated across cultures with similar results (Burger, 2009, found 70% compliance at a point equivalent to Milgram's maximum). However, Gina Perry's (2013) archival research suggests Milgram massaged his data — many participants in his own records doubted the experiment's authenticity, undermining the internal validity of the 'agentic state' explanation.

Minority Influence and Social Change

Groups are not only a source of conformity — they can be changed by determined minorities. Moscovici et al. (1969) showed that a consistent minority (confederates who repeatedly described blue slides as 'green') influenced 8.4% of participants' judgements. Key conditions for minority influence:

  • Consistency: Minorities must maintain their position over time — inconsistency is read as uncertainty.
  • Commitment: Making sacrifices for the cause signals conviction (the suffragettes, Greta Thunberg).
  • Flexibility: A minority that can adapt its messaging without abandoning core positions is more persuasive than a rigidly dogmatic one.

Minority influence tends to produce internalisation (genuine private attitude change) rather than mere compliance, making it the mechanism through which social change occurs — from same-sex marriage legislation to environmental activism.

Social Influence in Everyday Life

Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment (1971): Participants randomly assigned to 'prisoner' or 'guard' roles rapidly adopted corresponding behaviours — guards became authoritarian and abusive; prisoners became submissive and distressed. The experiment was terminated after 6 days. The findings suggest that situational roles, not individual character, drive much authoritarian behaviour. (Subsequent analysis, including Blum (2018) and Reicher & Haslam's critique, suggests considerable demand characteristics — guards were instructed to be tough — complicating the classic interpretation.)

Bystander effect: Darley and Latané (1968) demonstrated that the more people witness an emergency, the less likely any individual is to help — due to diffusion of responsibility (assuming someone else will intervene) and pluralistic ignorance (looking to others for cues about how to interpret an ambiguous situation, and all seeing others' apparent calm as a signal that nothing is wrong).

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen begins today with a clip: Asch's 1951 footage. The participant hesitates, looks down the row of confederates, then gives the wrong answer. The student sitting next to you shifts uncomfortably.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: What strikes you when you watch that? ... Yes — he knows the answer. You can see it in his face. But he still conforms. Why? Because humans are profoundly social animals. The discomfort of publicly disagreeing with a unanimous group triggers an ancient alarm — rejection, exclusion, being cast out. We evolved to be sensitive to group consensus, and our nervous systems respond accordingly.

storyBeats.speaker: Real-world obedience
storyBeats.text: In 2015, nurses in a French hospital television experiment were asked by a 'doctor' they had never met — speaking only by phone — to administer a clearly excessive drug dose to a patient. Despite having professional training, explicit instructions not to follow unverified phone orders, and no confirmation that the 'doctor' was genuine, 26 out of 27 nurses began preparing the overdose. The study was eventually stopped. Milgram's findings were not historical relics.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Social psychology has been called the most dangerous field in science — not because the research is dangerous, but because the findings make comfortable assumptions about human nature very difficult to maintain. The evidence suggests that it is not primarily character that determines whether someone obeys, conforms, or helps — it is situation. That should change how we design institutions, authority structures, and ethical training.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
In 2001, a group of nurses at a hospital were asked by a superior to falsify patient records to meet a performance target. Four nurses complied. One refused, raised the issue formally, and was subsequently excluded from team activities by her colleagues.

Using your knowledge of social influence research, explain:

  1. What psychological processes might explain why the four nurses who complied did so, even knowing it was wrong.
  2. What processes might explain the social reaction the nurse who refused experienced.
  3. What institutional changes could a hospital make to reduce the likelihood of this kind of compliance?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Several social influence processes may explain the four nurses' compliance. Normative social influence — the fear of social rejection and group exclusion if they refused — likely played a role, especially given the subsequent ostracism of the nurse who refused. Milgram's concept of the agentic state is also relevant: the nurses may have seen themselves as agents of their superior's authority, placing moral responsibility on the authority figure rather than themselves. The gradual escalation of commitment ('foot in the door') may also be relevant if smaller ethical compromises had been accepted previously, making this step feel less extreme. Finally, the unanimity of the group — if all four complied together — would have strengthened normative pressure through the appearance of consensus.

2. The refusal of one nurse — a minority of one — would have disrupted the group's unanimity, which Asch's research shows dramatically reduces conformity for others. The ostracism she experienced is consistent with social psychology's finding that groups punish deviants who threaten group cohesion, particularly when the deviance publicly exposes the group's behaviour. Her exclusion was a form of normative punishment, demonstrating the social costs of independence.

3. Institutional changes to reduce compliance with unethical orders include: (1) establishing clear ethical reporting pathways that protect whistleblowers from retaliation, reducing the personal cost of refusal; (2) dispersing rather than concentrating authority, so no single superior can create a culture of compliance without checks; (3) ethics training that specifically addresses obedience dynamics and teaches nurses to recognise and resist situational pressure; (4) introducing 'speaking up' culture through team briefings that explicitly normalise raising concerns; and (5) creating accountability structures where compliance with unethical orders has consequences, shifting the cost-benefit calculation.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Moscovici argued that social change is driven by consistent minorities, not by majorities. Evaluate this claim with reference to psychological research and at least one real-world historical example of minority-driven social change. In your answer, address: (1) what makes a minority influential; (2) how minority influence differs from conformity in its mechanisms; and (3) one limitation of the minority influence literature. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Moscovici et al.'s (1969) research demonstrated that a behavioural minority can influence the majority's perceptions — participants exposed to confederates consistently labelling blue slides as green showed a small but significant shift in their colour judgements. This suggests minorities can shift opinion through what Moscovici called the 'conversion effect': triggering systematic processing of an alternative viewpoint, leading to genuine private attitude change (internalisation) rather than mere public compliance.

For a minority to be influential, research suggests it must be consistent (maintaining its position across time and contexts), committed (making genuine sacrifices signals conviction rather than caprice), and flexible enough to adapt messaging without abandoning core principles. The women's suffrage movement exemplifies this: suffragettes maintained a consistent position on voting rights over decades, demonstrated extreme commitment through hunger strikes and imprisonment, and adapted tactics (from peaceful marches to property destruction) while never deviating from their core demand.

Minority influence differs from conformity in mechanism. Conformity (whether normative or informational) typically produces compliance without necessarily changing private beliefs — people go along with the majority without being truly persuaded. Minority influence, by contrast, tends to produce internalisation: the minority's consistent position prompts systematic re-evaluation, and attitude change is more durable.

One limitation: the minority influence literature has focused heavily on artificial laboratory tasks (colour judgements) with trivial stakes. Whether the same dynamics operate for high-stakes minority positions (political extremism, cult membership) with significant social costs for agreement is less clear.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why people sometimes do things in groups that they would never do on their own — use the Milgram study or the bystander effect as your main example, and explain what this tells us about the power of the situation versus individual character.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Milgram's term for the psychological state where a person sees themselves as an agent executing an authority's wishes, rather than as an autonomous moral agent responsible for their own actions.
The reduction in an individual's felt obligation to act when other people are present — each person assumes someone else will intervene, leading to collective inaction.
A situation where most members of a group privately reject a norm but go along with it because they incorrectly believe everyone else endorses it. Common in bystander situations.

A compliance strategy where a small initial request is made first; agreement to this increases the likelihood of later compliance with a larger request. Underlies the gradual escalation in Milgram's procedure.

Internalisation is genuine private attitude change; compliance is public agreement without private acceptance. Minority influence tends to produce internalisation; normative conformity produces compliance.

questions.questionHtml: In Asch's (1951) line studies, what percentage of participants conformed to the incorrect majority on at least one critical trial?
questions.explanationHtml: 75% of participants conformed on at least one trial — meaning three-quarters of people went along with the obviously wrong majority answer at some point. The overall conformity rate (proportion of critical trials on which participants gave the wrong answer) was approximately 32%. The 65% figure is Milgram's obedience finding (not Asch's conformity finding), and is a common confusion in exams.

questions.questionHtml: A group of office workers are asked by their manager to approve a budget that they privately believe is wasteful. They all sign it to avoid conflict, even though each privately disagrees. Which form of social influence best explains their behaviour?
questions.explanationHtml: The workers are conforming to avoid social conflict (disapproval from the manager) rather than because they believe the budget is correct — they privately disagree but publicly comply. This is normative social influence: conforming to expectations to avoid rejection or disapproval, without genuinely accepting the position. Informational influence involves genuinely believing the group knows better. Minority influence involves a small group shifting a majority's views. Internalisation involves genuine private attitude change — which is not occurring here.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Milgram's research showed that the majority of participants (over 50%) in his baseline condition administered the maximum 450-volt shock to the learner.
questions.explanationHtml: True. In Milgram's baseline condition (experimenter present in the room, learner in an adjacent room), 65% of participants administered the maximum 450-volt shock — well above 50%. This was a shocking result even to Milgram, who had predicted that only 1–3% would go all the way. The finding demonstrates the power of authority and situational factors in producing destructive obedience.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following best explains why minority influence tends to produce more durable attitude change than majority conformity?
options: Minorities use stronger social pressure than majorities
Minority positions provoke systematic thinking about the message, leading to internalisation rather than mere compliance
Majorities are always wrong about the issues they advocate for
Minorities are more consistent than majorities in their positions
questions.correctAnswer: Minority positions provoke systematic thinking about the message, leading to internalisation rather than mere compliance
questions.explanationHtml: Moscovici's dual-process account of social influence distinguishes between social comparison (the key process in majority conformity — we compare our position with others and adjust publicly to reduce conflict) and validation (the key process in minority influence — we are intrigued by the minority's confidence and engage in systematic processing of their argument). This deeper processing leads to internalisation (genuine belief change) rather than superficial compliance. Minority consistency is a condition for influence, not the explanation for why that influence is durable.

subChunks.title: Attitudes, Prejudice & Intergroup Relations
subChunks.hookHtml: In 1954, Kenneth and Mamie Clark testified before the United States Supreme Court in the case of Brown v. Board of Education, presenting research showing that Black children in segregated schools preferred to play with white dolls and attributed positive characteristics to white dolls and negative characteristics to Black ones. Their 'doll test' became central evidence that segregation caused psychological harm to Black children. The Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional. This is social psychology at its most consequential: research on attitudes and prejudice directly informing law. Understanding how attitudes form, how prejudice operates, and how intergroup conflict can be reduced is not only academically important — it is among the most practically urgent applications of psychological science.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Attitude Structure and the ABC Model

Attitudes are evaluative dispositions toward objects, people, or ideas. The ABC (tripartite) model holds that attitudes have three components:

Affective   — emotional response ('I feel disgusted by...')
Behavioural — tendency to act in certain ways ('I avoid...')
Cognitive   — beliefs about the attitude object ('I think that...')

These components may be inconsistent. LaPiere (1934) found that hotel and restaurant owners expressed anti-Chinese attitudes in questionnaires but served a Chinese couple in 250 real-world visits. The attitude-behaviour gap — discrepancy between expressed attitudes and actual behaviour — is explained by situational factors, social norms, and the specificity of the attitude measure.

Elaboration Likelihood Model (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986): Attitudes can be changed via two routes: the central route (careful processing of message quality, leading to durable attitude change) or the peripheral route (using heuristics like 'this person seems credible', leading to superficial and temporary change). Which route is taken depends on motivation and ability to process the message.

Prejudice and Discrimination

Prejudice: a pre-formed, often negative attitude toward a social group, not based on personal experience. Discrimination: the behavioural expression of prejudice — unequal treatment of individuals based on group membership. Stereotypes: overgeneralised beliefs about a group, which may be positive or negative but are always an oversimplification.

Allport (1954) proposed a five-step escalation scale of prejudice expression:

1. Antilocution    — verbal abuse, derogatory jokes
2. Avoidance       — avoiding contact with outgroup members
3. Discrimination  — active exclusion from opportunities
4. Physical attack — hate crimes, violence
5. Extermination   — genocide

Origins of Prejudice

Social Identity Theory (Tajfel & Turner, 1979)

People derive self-esteem from membership in social groups (ingroups). To maintain positive social identity, they engage in ingroup favouritism (evaluating the ingroup positively) and outgroup derogation (evaluating outgroups negatively). Tajfel's minimal group paradigm demonstrated that mere categorisation into arbitrary groups (even on the basis of coin flips) was sufficient to produce ingroup favouritism — suggesting that intergroup bias does not require competition or a history of conflict.

Realistic Conflict Theory (Sherif, 1954)

The Robbers Cave experiment: two groups of boys at a summer camp, after being placed in competition for limited resources (a trophy, prizes), developed strong intergroup hostility and prejudice. When competition was replaced with cooperation to achieve superordinate goals (goals requiring both groups' effort), hostility reduced. This suggests that competition for scarce resources drives prejudice, and cooperation reduces it.

Reducing Prejudice: The Contact Hypothesis

Allport (1954) proposed that intergroup contact reduces prejudice, but only under certain conditions:

  • Equal status: groups must meet as equals, not in subordinate/dominant roles.
  • Common goals: working together toward shared objectives.
  • Cooperation: rather than competition.
  • Institutional support: authorities (governments, schools, employers) endorse the contact.

Meta-analyses (Pettigrew & Tropp, 2006) confirm that contact under these conditions reduces prejudice, though effects vary by group and context. Programmes such as the Jigsaw Classroom (Aronson, 1971) — where children are made interdependent for learning tasks — have been successfully applied in desegregated schools.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen is running a live demonstration. She asks students to stand up if they are wearing blue. Then if they wear glasses. Then to sit back down if they've ever been unfairly treated because of how they look. The room is uncomfortably quiet.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Prejudice is not exotic. It's the default setting of a cognitive system that evolved to quickly categorise threats. 'Ingroup or outgroup? Friend or stranger?' That categorisation becomes prejudice when it's applied rigidly, emotionally, and in contexts where it causes harm. Social identity theory says we don't even need a history of conflict — just the word 'us' and the word 'them' is enough.

storyBeats.speaker: Minimal groups in practice
storyBeats.text: Tajfel divided Bristol schoolboys into groups ostensibly based on their preference for Klee vs. Kandinsky paintings — but the assignment was actually random. Even in this minimal, meaningless group, boys allocated more resources to their ingroup members and less to outgroup members. They had met for minutes. They had no history of conflict. They did it anyway.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: The optimistic implication is that contact can undo what categorisation creates — but not any contact. Contact between unequals often reinforces prejudice. The conditions matter: equal status, cooperation toward shared goals, institutional backing. The Jigsaw Classroom works because each child is genuinely needed for the group to succeed. Dependency on the outgroup member is not something prejudice can easily survive.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A school is experiencing tension between two groups of students: a long-established local community and newly arrived migrant students. Staff have noticed that students from each group sit separately at lunch, avoid one another in corridors, and spread negative rumours about the other group.

Drawing on Allport's contact hypothesis and Sherif's realistic conflict theory:

  1. Identify which conditions for reducing prejudice are currently absent in this school environment.
  2. Design two specific interventions — one drawing on the contact hypothesis, one drawing on realistic conflict theory — that the school could implement to reduce intergroup tension.
  3. Predict one obstacle that might reduce the effectiveness of each intervention.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Allport's contact hypothesis requires equal status, common goals, cooperation, and institutional support. Currently, several of these conditions appear absent. Equal status is uncertain — newly arrived migrant students may have lower social status in the school hierarchy. Common goals are absent: separate seating and avoidance suggest students are pursuing individual group goals, not working toward shared objectives. Cooperation is clearly absent (the groups avoid each other). Institutional support may be lacking if staff are not actively modelling and enforcing positive intergroup norms.

2. Contact hypothesis intervention: Introduce structured mixed-group project work in lessons, where groups contain both local and migrant students and each student is assigned a distinct role essential to the project's success (a 'jigsaw' structure). This creates cooperation toward a common goal between students of equal academic status, under teacher supervision and endorsement — meeting all four of Allport's conditions. Realistic conflict theory intervention: Identify a genuine challenge facing all students regardless of group (e.g., a fundraising goal, a sports competition against another school) and frame it as a superordinate goal requiring collective effort. This replaces intergroup competition with intergroup cooperation, which Sherif found dramatically reduces hostility.

3. Obstacle for the contact intervention: Students who bring strong existing prejudices from their home environment may resist working with outgroup members and use the group-work setting to express rather than reduce hostility — particularly if the teacher does not actively facilitate positive interaction and address negative behaviour immediately. Obstacle for the superordinate goal intervention: If the goal is not genuinely shared — if one group feels the outcome matters more to them than to the other — the sense of common fate required for prejudice reduction may not materialise. Migrant students who do not feel fully part of the school community may not feel motivated by goals that seem oriented to the established student body.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Social identity theory and realistic conflict theory offer competing explanations for the origins of prejudice. Compare these two theories, evaluate the evidence for each, and discuss which provides a more complete account of intergroup conflict. Aim for 200–250 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
Social identity theory (SIT; Tajfel & Turner, 1979) proposes that prejudice arises from the fundamental human need for positive self-esteem derived from group membership. Because ingroup members are motivated to view their group favourably, they automatically derogate outgroups to achieve positive distinctiveness. Tajfel's minimal group paradigm demonstrates that mere categorisation — with no history of competition or interaction — produces ingroup favouritism, supporting SIT's claim that conflict is not required for prejudice.

Realistic conflict theory (RCT; Sherif, 1966) takes a different position: prejudice and hostility arise from genuine competition between groups for limited resources. The Robbers Cave experiment provides compelling evidence — intergroup hostility escalated when boys competed for scarce prizes and reduced when competition was replaced by superordinate goals. RCT is supported by historical patterns: ethnic and racial tensions often intensify during economic downturns when competition for jobs and resources increases.

SIT offers the more parsimonious account — it explains why prejudice occurs even without competition, which RCT cannot readily accommodate. However, RCT has strong ecological validity and better explains the escalation and reduction of prejudice over time in real-world contexts. The two theories are complementary: SIT explains the minimal conditions under which intergroup bias emerges, while RCT explains why prejudice intensifies under competition and diminishes under cooperation. A complete account of intergroup conflict likely requires both.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what prejudice actually is — how it forms, and why people can be prejudiced without realising it. Use one piece of psychological research to back up your explanation.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Attitudes or stereotypes that affect judgment without conscious awareness, measured by tools like the Implicit Association Test (IAT). Contrasts with explicit attitudes expressed consciously.
Tajfel & Turner's (1979) theory that people derive self-esteem from their social group memberships, leading to ingroup favouritism and outgroup derogation to achieve positive distinctiveness.
Goals that transcend group boundaries and require cooperation between groups to achieve. Sherif's Robbers Cave experiment showed these reduce intergroup hostility more effectively than mere contact.

Steele & Aronson's (1995) finding that awareness of a negative stereotype about one's group can impair performance in the stereotyped domain — e.g., Black students performing worse on tests when race is made salient.

questions.questionHtml: According to Allport's contact hypothesis, which of the following conditions is NOT required for contact between groups to reduce prejudice?
options: Competition between the groups for shared resources
questions.correctAnswer: Competition between the groups for shared resources
questions.explanationHtml: Allport's contact hypothesis specifies four conditions for contact to reduce prejudice: equal status, common goals, cooperation, and institutional support. Competition is the opposite of what is required — it is a driver of prejudice in Sherif's realistic conflict theory. Introducing competition between groups would be expected to increase rather than reduce intergroup hostility.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Tajfel's minimal group paradigm showed that prejudice and discrimination require a history of conflict or competition between groups to develop.
questions.explanationHtml: False. The minimal group paradigm specifically demonstrates that mere categorisation into arbitrary, meaningless groups (based on painting preferences or coin flips) is sufficient to produce ingroup favouritism and outgroup discrimination — even with no history of conflict, no prior interaction, and no realistic competition. This finding is the core challenge to realistic conflict theory: prejudice does not require material conditions to emerge.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher finds that adults who scored higher on an explicit prejudice measure against elderly people also behaved more slowly and dismissively when giving directions to an elderly confederate. However, the correlation between explicit prejudice and behaviour was only r = 0.28. Which of the following best explains this modest relationship?
options: Explicit attitude measures are not valid
The attitude-behaviour gap — situational factors moderate the expression of attitudes in behaviour
Prejudice against elderly people is less severe than other forms of prejudice
The sample size was probably too small to detect a true relationship
questions.correctAnswer: The attitude-behaviour gap — situational factors moderate the expression of attitudes in behaviour
questions.explanationHtml: The attitude-behaviour gap — the observation that expressed attitudes often imperfectly predict behaviour — is well documented (LaPiere, 1934). Situational factors such as social norms (it may not be socially acceptable to be obviously dismissive), competing motivations (wanting to appear helpful), and the specificity of the situation all moderate how much attitudes translate into behaviour. The modest r = 0.28 does not indicate the measure is invalid — it reflects the genuine complexity of the attitude-behaviour relationship. The other options are less compelling explanations of the modest correlation.
